findings.observation: Fortification measured 286 m with nine towers. Wall 1 clearly exposed only in D5; Wall 2 precedes towers; Wall 3 abuts towers; outer mantle abuts Wall 3. Surface pottery/coins have no sealed construction association. Five architectural stages documented.
findings.author_interpretation: Three/four absolute chronological phases and First Revolt/Bar Kokhba correlations are author reconstructions; tower typology alone does not anchor chronology.
findings.project_inference: Retain architectural ordering separately from historical event dates. The 8 m southern gap in D1 lacks an identified original terminus and cannot be assigned as an ancient entrance.

findings.observation: 171 caves detected, 119 surveyed/mapped; note 14 refers to 53 additional unsurveyed caves, which does not equal the difference of 52. Coordinates explicitly Old Israel Grid; slope caves received no elevations. Cave 137 and natural Cave 143 are described as accessible by climbing from the cliff foot, whereas 138–140 require rappelling.
findings.author_interpretation: Cliff shelters generally described as accessible solely by ropes, but individual appendix entries preserve exceptions. Two restorable T1.3 jars in Cistern II provide typological late first-century BCE/early first-century CE evidence.
findings.project_inference: Keep catalogue-specific access statements, count discrepancy and survey coverage limits. Surface pottery or cistern contents cannot establish a sealed construction phase for an entire cave complex.

findings.observation: B6 burnt-house hoard of 60 coins found clumped at wall/pier corner. Latest silver denarius no392 dated end 125 CE; separate worn provincial bronze no435 bears Legio VI countermarks, assigned circa 123–135 CE. Catalogue preserves these as distinct coins.
findings.author_interpretation: Original pouch inferred; concealment upstairs/in ceiling explicitly speculative.
findings.project_inference: Record discovery location separately from inferred original hiding place; TPQ from latest issue does not identify a particular destruction year.

findings.observation: Pottery quantified as identifiable rim fragments, matching fragments counted once; approximately 9,000 identified vessels/fragments, 8,839 diagnostic rims in Table 9.1. Only types with four or more examples discussed systematically. Counts include acknowledged intrusive material.
findings.author_interpretation: Relative type frequencies interpreted for household function, settlement intensity and production centers.
findings.project_inference: Do not present these counts as an estimated whole-vessel population or equate rare-type omission with absence. Connector tables are flattened; columns require native verification before numeric reuse.

findings.observation: Four soundings are fully sealed beneath surviving floors/bedding; A3 disturbed and part of A1 missing floor. Terrace fill primarily Early Roman. Later intrusions associated with column foundations, drain, mosaic bedding and east-wall trench are distinguished. Northwest floor finds under collapse include coin of 364–375 CE and Early Byzantine ceramics.
findings.author_interpretation: Synagogue I early third century and II late third/very early fourth inferred from specific construction intrusions; late floor finds interpreted as washed in after abandonment and before final collapse (possibly 419 CE).
findings.project_inference: Keep terrace, construction interventions, abandonment and collapse separate; under-debris location does not automatically establish occupation date or original deposit.

findings.observation: Stone corpus comprises 163 artifacts. Water basin no134 is surface find L1A999, roughly 10 m southeast of synagogue entrance, capacity approximately 60 liters; no in situ connection to a supply/drain network. Chalkstone krater no133 recovered in Hadrianic destruction, surviving profile with convex base; foot not preserved.
findings.author_interpretation: Basin interpreted for washing hands/feet by comparative placement and literary evidence. Krater trumpet-foot reconstructed by analogies; water storage inferred by parallels. Qalal identification rejected because term describes function rather than a particular shape.
findings.project_inference: Surface find does not locate an original basin station or establish a hydraulic system. Do not convert chalkstone mugs to measuring cups; exact material/stratum labels vary across catalogue and plate tables and need native verification.

findings.observation: 33 common restorable vessels sampled from Hadrianic destruction: 20 cooking vessels, 11 storage jars and two jugs. Seventeen cooking samples match characteristic Kefar Hananya micromorphology; three have weak/inactive birefringence but compatible minerals and no known alternative signature. All 13 non-cooking samples statistically consistent with Shikhin group.
findings.author_interpretation: Kefar Hananya/Shikhin identified as dominant suppliers; possible transport routes and jar marketing purposes inferred.
findings.project_inference: Do not generalize sampled common/restorable pottery to every vessel or treat suggested route as an excavated ancient road. Hotelling multivariate-normality assumption deferred by authors to a later study (note41 p413).

findings.observation: Mount Nitai metal finds largely lack clear stratigraphy; catalogue includes medieval arrowhead no83, Ottoman musket balls no84, probable Byzantine/later arrowheads nos81–82. Raptor nests observed; cave lead objects could have been transported by birds. Arrowhead no76 embedded in Cave45 wall, bent tip/tang; no independent sealed date.
findings.author_interpretation: Some low-quality arrowheads assigned tentatively to Jewish rebels; shot direction/crossbow inferred from impact and mass. Hobnail no89 compatible with soldiers and civilians.
findings.project_inference: Do not assign all cave metal to a single Roman event or infer military occupation from a hobnail alone. Mixed modern finds omitted from ancient-object counts; raptor transport is a possible formation process, not demonstrated provenance.

findings.observation: P471 calls the no-later-than late-fourth/early-fifth-century use bound a terminus post quem. P470 refers to mold-blown grape bottle as no70, while catalogue no61 is the grape bottle and no70 a blue-trailed neck. Lamp bowl no72 catalogue location is beneath topsoil; other lamp fragments include wash/topsoil/baulk contexts.
findings.author_interpretation: Lamp-bowl forms associated with final synagogue stage; glass chronological extension based on stratigraphy and typology.
findings.project_inference: Preserve published wording but logically distinguish an ante quem usage bound from TPQ deposition. Use catalogue identity/context; do not give every fragment sealed-destruction status.

findings.observation: A11 nos447–448 labelled intrusive; dispersed coins omitted from hoard may originally belong. Burnt-room nos436,438,446 sieved from L4A046; table notes say maybe belong to Unit A11 hoard despite different discovery area. Agrippa II no129 prose dated88/89, catalogue allows77/78 or88/89 and note15 favors77/78. A reported1972 First Revolt silver hoard rests on personal communication/purchased coins, not excavation context.
findings.author_interpretation: B6/A5 destruction linked probably to Bar Kokhba Revolt; A11 interpreted as synagogue congregational savings rather than emergency deposit. Mint profile interpreted as economic/administrative ties.
findings.project_inference: Latest coins give deposition TPQ; revolt connection, emergency purpose, congregational ownership and Tiberias administrative jurisdiction remain interpretations. Preserve uncertain hoard membership and competing eras. Reported market hoard cannot substitute for securely located excavation evidence.

findings.observation: Complete locus index labels all elevations m asl, yet values use village arbitrary +100 m benchmark and separate mountain +10 m benchmarks. Critical loci are marked by bold typography, lost in plain extraction. Entries include reversed opening/closing values (e.g.1A006 99.17/99.81 p637;4A033 98.70/98.73 p643;5A222 96.32/96.78 p648;5A228 95.82/95.87 p649), and self-referential relations (3A009,3A015 p640;6A001 p649).
findings.author_interpretation: Index compiles excavation registration rather than a single newly harmonized stratigraphic sequence.
findings.project_inference: Retain explicit local-datum conversion despite index header. Do not machine-build a Harris graph or certify critical-locus status from flattened extraction; verify bold marking, relation typos and elevations in native pages first.

findings.observation: Mountain coins range fourth-century BCE to modern; Cave32 drachm dated334–325/4 BCE in prose, table334–324/3, and note10 reports chronological markers invalid and suggests324/3. Fatimid dinar1017 CE in rock niche Cave28 and separate bronze weight Cave167. Weight50.01 g after conservation versus50.92 before.
findings.author_interpretation: Dinar deliberately hidden; single-coin deposit or surviving fragment of old hoard alternatives. Refugees from Tiberias and particular eleventh-century events suggested. Weight17 dirhams or12 dinars offered as alternatives to expected20-dirham standard.
findings.project_inference: Keep updated note rather than fixed early drachm date. Concealment observation does not establish original hoard size, refugee origin or historic event. Do not collapse competing weight standards.

findings.observation: No paint/stucco fragments found in situ; complete original decorative schemes unavailable. Amulet lamella11×5 cm and case6×2 cm in chapter19, versus10.5×5 cm and6×2 mm case in chapter14 p498. Five lines mostly magic signs/pseudoletters; tentative name/in-the-name reading of line2 only.
findings.author_interpretation: Amulet function identified by technical parallels; pseudoletters-to-Aramaic-text development expressly speculative. Early public-building identification and decorative source reconstructed from fragments.
findings.project_inference: Preserve conflicting measurements and uncertainty of inscription readings. Do not treat a metal lamella as a legible documentary text or reconstruct whole wall schemes from isolated fragments.

findings.observation: No village cistern or ritual bath discovered. Underground chambers lack plaster and original function unknown. Cemetery caves and nearby sarcophagi/cist tombs surveyed; attribution to village inferred from proximity, several lack independent date anchors.
findings.author_interpretation: Early public structure probably synagogue; chambers storage/hiding alternatives; spring possibly used for immersion. Bar Kokhba linkage one possibility, local unrest before revolt retained. Village decline starts before363 CE and economic factors proposed.
findings.project_inference: Keep inferred building function, refuge roles, settlement population estimates (40/30 dunams multiplied by20 people per dunam), and regional cemetery ownership separate from excavated observations. No evidence here identifies a Copper Scroll deposit.

findings.observation: Most605temenos lamps from mixed dumping operations filling T1 podium at least twice, possibly three times;105from northern settlement not directly connected to temple. Ash/bone niche deposit includes coin dated54 CE (p109note331). Altar no clear stratigraphic building assignment. Table3.17p125 repeats M4.5.3185/8, /9 and /14 rows.
findings.author_interpretation: Lamps near altar and ash/bone deposit interpreted ritual; sheer quantity used to reject personal construction-worker lamps. Sanctuary use, offerings and banquets discussed by analogy, exact practices unknown.
findings.project_inference: Do not convert redeposited lamps to original ritual/hiding stations. Check denominator/duplicated table rows before totals. ES circa30 BCE architectural-style date remains an inference and cannot be proven by broad lamp typology.

findings.observation: P118 claims all BetSheanType30 lamps occur only in temenos C8/D8 and none in northern settlement through2011. Table3.15 explicitly titled northern settlement through2011 lists Type30 at M11.4.56, M11.4.66/1, M11.10.116, M11.11.119, N11.4.28, N13.7.086, O11.1.86/89, O11.2.90 and O11.5.94.
findings.author_interpretation: Late fourth/early fifth-century modifications inferred from lamp dates.
findings.project_inference: Preserve contradiction and require native/table/context cross-check before asserting geographic absence. Plate/caption reconstruction cannot repair chronology or provenance.

findings.observation: Large figurine fragments occur in secondary deposits emptied and refilled during T2 construction or repair. No reconstruction of individual complete figures was possible; estimated 20–40 originals. Editors note that the togate relief has a different arm pose, closed palm and held object.
findings.author_interpretation: Child rites of passage, healing or thanksgiving cult, nearby manufacture and individual portraits are proposed. Editors offer a civic official with race-starting mappa as a relief parallel.
findings.project_inference: Do not localize the original ritual or assign it to ES/T1 from redistributed fragments. Cult and production hypotheses are not excavated original placement or workshop evidence.

findings.observation: Block C20.7 is assigned by Nelson to T2 by dimensions/provenance but Rozenberg favors an earlier reused block by plaster and style. Most loose fragments came from fills. The lozenge fresco was damaged in the container fire; only low-resolution photographs of its original color/design survive.
findings.author_interpretation: Four plaster types may reflect different periods or different teams. Cinnabar/celadonite import and local Egyptian-blue production are inferred from composition.
findings.project_inference: Preserve competing attribution and fill-context limits. These decorative plaster types do not directly establish waterproof lining or a connected water system.

findings.observation: Table6.1 lists seven Tyre coins without CN18; Table6.2 gives eight and CN18 catalogue identifies Tyre. CN70 and CN72 repeat IAA102592, diameter24mm and weight5.40g while their registration/type differ. CN23, CN59 and CN67 have printed diameter0.
findings.author_interpretation: A continuous issued-coin sequence is interpreted as no occupation gap; CN1 temple similarity supports Augusteum identification.
findings.project_inference: Catalogue inconsistencies require native verification before quantitative reuse. Issue dates and widespread coin imagery alone do not establish continuous use, route or uniquely identify the pictured temple.

findings.observation: Two pipes north of T2 north parastade niche; lower molding cut for pipe. Channel on south backing block continues down to behind third stair course then across toward south parastade. Southern niche is not extant; only beginning of channel there. Transition from propylon ramp to paving unexcavated. Native Figs7.7–7.11 inspected individually.
findings.author_interpretation: Paired niche fountains with Echo statues linked to pavement benefaction are reconstructed. North-to-south flow favored but reverse flow possible (note34); no south feed/drain trace. Reading of cuttings, abbreviations and donation debated, including note19 alternative paved.
findings.project_inference: Observed channels support a local conduit; paired fountains, statuary, connection to inscription and complete source/outlet are conditional. Do not promote a water-display reconstruction into a fully surveyed water route.

findings.observation: Large burnt deposit lacks extensive adjacent fresco burning and contains unburnt building inclusions. BN142/153 reattributed after study to T2 construction, while retained ES table9.39 and BN152 attribution complicate cross-table joins. SP5-4 burning is BN65/66/68 in text/Table9.21–22 but BN66/67/68 in Tables9.2–3.
findings.author_interpretation: Offering burnt elsewhere and swiftly buried is tentative; Roman purification/foundation offering favored from architectural context. Jewish ritual parallels do not identify the practitioners.
findings.project_inference: Preserve depositional versus burning location and revised phase distinction. Printed p236 counts 56 black/131 unburnt differ from Table9.10 p252 (61 carbonized black,125 unburnt); verify before exact reuse.

findings.observation: Sphinx recovered in SP1 fill reopened in Byzantine phase, with uncertain original function. Marble analysis combines isotopes and grain/structure, favoring Paros Marathi. Neo-Assyrian seal SF55 found in Roman fill. Stucco-head placement differs between Nelson pediment and Erlich lower display proposals.
findings.author_interpretation: Sphinx Asiatic workshop/style, third-century arrival and entrance/bench placement proposed. Seal arrival with Sargon II official and later grave recovery or votive reuse are hypotheses.
findings.project_inference: Raw-material source is not workshop/location; portable-object style/date does not prove contemporary site occupation, military route or original ritual placement.

findings.observation: L23.7 basin/pipe P9 assigned6th–8thc at182.47m; O12.12 P8 assigned4th–5thc at184.08m; N22.5 covering pipes is ND. Table a.45 SP4-4.13 opens180.80/closes180.75 whereas Table1.4 p24 opens180.00. B11.3 opening181.28 closing181.50 reversed; M6.5(2007)180.4/181.15 reversed. O12.9 and SP1.50 print50–100bce despite Early Roman pottery.
findings.author_interpretation: Appendix separates pottery dates and locus assigned dates; surface contaminants, unexcavated fills and cleaning defined explicitly.
findings.project_inference: Do not combine late P8/P9 basin system with first-century niche system. Retain table variants; no automatic depth/chronology repair or sealed-locus assumption.

findings.observation: Two podium chambers have visible joint mortar, concrete floor above them and a connecting passage. Chamber floors remain covered by unexcavated earth. Shaft-cover block C24.3 was found displaced in SP5; its 16 cm rebate matches the concrete floor thickness. Native p362 figures587–588 now inspected: catalogue labels C24.3/A1297 Wellhead, ES2, findspot1:SP5; photograph/state drawing show broken circular opening with dashed restored circumference, and a separately labelled1:2 front-face crown-molding profile.
findings.author_interpretation: Chambers might have served a funerary or cistern function; block C24.3 may have secured the squared opening in the floor. Concrete sealing might prevent evaporation or rainwater ingress.
findings.project_inference: Do not record confirmed cistern use, water-tightness or storage capacity without excavated chamber floors and demonstrated hydraulic function.

findings.observation: Temenos pavement elevations slope southwest; much southwestern paving is missing. A step channel reaches the northern parastade; a separate vertical channel is cut on its north face. Only portions of the propylon were excavated.
findings.author_interpretation: Southwestern rainwater collection drain presumed; lead pipe in parastade channel proposed. Temenos extent 62×85 m inferred from aerial troughs and axial symmetry; partly hypaethral roof considered.
findings.project_inference: Preserve inferred drain and perimeter separately from excavated channels and surviving pipes documented in volume II. Temple rainwater collection devices remain unknown because later activity removed floor/subfloor.

findings.observation: Site north is a roughly 20-degree counterclockwise descriptive rotation; temples face S69°35′45″E. More than 5000 fragments estimated, 576 diagnostic blocks inventoried and 265 catalogued; podium/paving blocks excluded. Many blocks moved during excavation. Text C2.1 drum diameters 0.338/0.370 m differ from table/catalogue 0.345/0.360 m. Figure 63 identifies C15.2=A1454, while table/catalogue identifies C15.24=A1454 and C15.2=A0089; figure 76 calls A1124 C15.17, but catalogue identifies C15.7=A1124 and C15.17=A1365.
findings.author_interpretation: Original block placement reconstructed partly from assumed near-vertical fall and architectural proportions. Unknown/preserved dimensions explicitly distinguished.
findings.project_inference: No millimetre-precision feature matching or automatic phase assignment from caption IDs; retain inventory IDs, original versus moved locations, and discrepancies for native verification.

findings.observation: Appendix C describes differentially corrected Trimble/OmniSTAR GNSS control, total-station closed corrected traverse and field drawing methods. Table 12 UTM36N control points: A1 N3678674.317 E748176.871 elevation182.856; B N3678651.400 E748194.300 elevation183.040; T N3678662.079 E748196.942 elevation183.703; DELTA N3678734.289 E748221.315 elevation182.932; C N3678645.150 E748211.103 elevation181.249.
findings.author_interpretation: Surveyed positions tie field drawings and blocks to three-dimensional coordinates. Finished dimensions measured to millimetres, preserved dimensions to centimetres.
findings.project_inference: Correct prior Omrit I datum-absent inference. Survey-point A1 differs from volume II southwestern excavation-grid corner A1; preserve reference roles and never substitute coordinates based on repeated name.
findings.native_verification: Physical403/405 native tables12–14 inspected; confirms published numbers and prose caveats. Native Table12 confirms A1 N3678674.317 E748176.871 elevation182.856; C N3678645.150 E748211.103 elevation181.249. Native Table14 prints identical W576.51kN/m for T1/T2, same E/CS/TS assumptions, but Dlow/high0.48/0.29 versus0.59/0.35mm and MaxTS2.45 versus3.02MPa. Paragraph expressly excludes roof weight.

findings.observation: No central arch or architrave backer found. Appendix D models reconstructed 5.13 m span using architrave plus backer as one homogeneous lintel, assumed limestone properties and uniformly distributed stone load. Calculation explicitly excludes roof weight although p68 summarizes support for entablature, pediment and roof. Table14 repeats W576.51 for T1 and T2 while deflection/stress results differ.
findings.author_interpretation: Simple lintel could span the central opening; arch unnecessary under stated model.
findings.project_inference: Capacity is conditional engineering reconstruction, not measured original structural performance. Do not use a presumed archive/lintel span as an excavated dimension without preserving assumptions.
findings.native_verification: Physical403/405 native tables12–14 inspected; confirms published numbers and prose caveats. Native Table12 confirms A1 N3678674.317 E748176.871 elevation182.856; C N3678645.150 E748211.103 elevation181.249. Native Table14 prints identical W576.51kN/m for T1/T2, same E/CS/TS assumptions, but Dlow/high0.48/0.29 versus0.59/0.35mm and MaxTS2.45 versus3.02MPa. Paragraph expressly excludes roof weight.

findings.observation: Native figure30 p107 caption calls south parastades but image labels say T1/T2 North Parastade. Figure46 p118 places A1492 at pediment apex whereas p33 identifies C4.16 (A1448) there. Figure58 p124 labels C12.2 (A1463) although table/catalogue links A1463 to C12.23 and C12.2 to A1171. Figure61 p125 labels C1.4 (A1458) although catalogue C1.4=A1486 and C1.2=A1458. Figure74 p132 states A1214 has no table entry, but Table22 p180 lists it among interior cella drums. Figure108 p148 says west temenos wall while photo label and location show east wall. Figure124 p155 caption identifies Structure D, but photo label identifies Structure E. Native catalogue p195 figures178–179 identify the angled front of C4.16/A1448; p196 figures181–182 identify C4.18/A1492 with straight front. Figure63 p126 labels C15.2/A1454 although catalogue C15.24=A1454 and C15.2=A0089. Figure76 p133 labels C15.17/A1124 although catalogue C15.7=A1124 and C15.17=A1365. Native catalogue p244 figures314–315 identify C12.23/A1463; native p228 figures274–275 identify C12.2/A1171. Native catalogue p260 fig358 confirms C15.2/A0089; p263 figs366–367 confirm C15.7/A1124; pp268–269 figs385–386 confirm C15.17/A1365; p272 figs399–400 confirm C15.24/A1454.
findings.author_interpretation: Text reconstructs positions and phase relations using mouldings and block context.
findings.project_inference: Use actual inventory identifiers and stated contextual relations; published captions require cross-checking before drawing feature-specific geometric or chronological conclusions. Remaining native figures still pending.

findings.observation: The detail profile in figure295 is explicitly labelled molding profile (not to scale); figure301 is explicitly labelled crown molding profile (not to scale). Photograph and state drawing group C14.6+C14.7+C14.8 (A1266+A1269+A1270) as fragments of a column base; separate catalogue entries refer to the same figures. Figures362,364,393 and428 explicitly show upside-down blocks; figure432 labels a top broken face and figure438 a bottom face.
findings.author_interpretation: Catalogue labels these as state drawings and identifies grouped fragments; enlarged profiles explicitly have no scale.
findings.project_inference: Their detail profiles cannot be measured using the scale bars attached to the adjacent state drawings. Shared photograph/drawing is one grouped original observation, not independent corroboration for each catalogue number. Preserve photograph orientation and broken versus original faces before geometric use.

findings.observation: In each native state drawing, both the narrow side/profile view and the main fascia elevation carry the printed label FRONT. Figure476 is C17.16/A1247; figure480 is C17.18/A1479.

findings.observation: In Field III.4, underground shaft/pit L 4032 was excavated incompletely several metres beneath Byzantine floor 679.75 m. Its northern rock wall has a lamp niche; there was no indication of burial. It connects to larger chamber L 4040 and a possible chamber L 4041. L 4032, 4037 and 4038 contain Early–Middle Roman pottery, chalkstone fragments and Herodian nozzles. More underground chambers lie east of wall 4015. A drain against the exterior of wall 1003 leads south toward an apparent outlet in 4012. The southern two-room building measures 4.8 × 3.25 m and 4.82 × 1.88 m; a modern burial beside 1015 disturbed the area.
findings.author_interpretation: The supervisor proposed a former tomb because of the niche. Authors retain that uncertainty, suggest filling and sealing in Period III, and say these chambers likely are those that collapsed and were later observed by Aviam. Room use and earlier above-ground configuration remain conjectural. Access from the south and east remains unexcavated; subsequent restoration impedes testing it.
findings.project_inference: These passages supply primary excavation evidence for incompletely investigated subterranean spaces. They supplement the earlier Aviam discussion without establishing his pre-revolt refuge chronology or a measured complete tunnel network.

findings.observation: Field IV rock-cut room has Early Roman occupational debris L 1017 and composite L 1020. Northern L 1020 includes occupation, collapse and leveling components that could not be separated stratigraphically. At floor level pit 1023 has diameter 1.4 m and bottom elevation 676.295 m, 45 cm below the room floor. Oval basin 1025 lies 50 cm south, is 1.25 m long and 5–10 cm deep, and has visible width about 50 cm. Pit 2044 is 1.95 m deep and 1.4 m in diameter. Adjacent 1030 is 68 cm deep and 52 cm wide, with plaster; 2046 is 43 × 72 cm and 40 cm deep, without plaster. Pit 2045 is 75 cm deep and 38 cm in diameter. A central bedrock pillar with ashlars rises 1.55 m. The L 1009 floor room measures 3.25 × 6 m. Text p. 125 prints southern room dimensions 2.5 × 28 m, inconsistent with surrounding geometry. Text p. 121 places filling of pit 2044 in Early Roman occupation; p. 128 places it in the Middle Roman expansion.
findings.author_interpretation: Authors infer a cistern or storage predecessor for 1023, an Early Roman chamber, and a Middle Roman rebuild. Hydraulic basin 1030 and unplastered basin 2046 form a suggested system for handling liquids. Household use and wider production or distribution remain alternatives. The courtyard and entrances were largely unexcavated; complete plan and function await further work.
findings.project_inference: Native Figures 30–31, sections and photos are still needed to check location and fine labels. Preserve the literal 28 m reading and conflicting fill-date passages. Early–Middle Roman ceramic ranges do not fix a pre-70 CE construction date.

findings.observation: The lamp chapter reports 48 lamps or fragments, 31 from critical loci, including 15 Herodian nozzles and three Darom fragments. Herodian types can continue to the mid-second century. Most lamps came from floor makeup, fill, a tabun or pit fill; neither clay nor glass lamps were found in primary synagogue contexts. Two potential Cypriot imports await chemical or petrographic analysis. Lapp did not examine B:3 or B:9. B:1 and C:3 are dated late eighth to early ninth century; C:2 has a seventh–ninth-century catalogue range. A:12 gives field II.4 for L 4032, although narrative identifies III.4. C:9 locus differs between catalogue and plate key (2006 versus 2005).
findings.author_interpretation: Lapp proposes limited external contact from lamp types. Directors explicitly qualify this in footnote 1 on p. 262, noting excavation in public space, coins from external trade centres and their own conclusion of considerable contact. Suggested origin of Herodian, Darom and discus lamps relies on comparison with analyses of material from other sites; Nabratein sourcing remains untested.
findings.project_inference: A Herodian nozzle alone cannot date deposition before 70 CE. Keep vessel age, context date, origin hypothesis and trade inference separate. Later lamp dates and explicit disagreement about isolation must remain visible.

findings.observation: The ground-stone corpus comprises 72 objects or fragments. Dating by tool form is limited because many types persist for long periods. Origin analysis was not performed. Fragmentary mortars and vessels cannot always be separated by macroscopic wear. Four handstones lack provenance and are excluded from the catalogue. The two basalt tables show grinding wear. Registration numbers differ between Chart 9 and plate keys in several entries; table 80559 has I.5.74 provenance in Plate C but IV.1.74 in Chart 9. Plate D calls d basalt vesicular although other keys define it as dense.
findings.author_interpretation: Local stone origin, household processing and an industrial role for tables are author interpretations; origins are inferred from availability rather than tested geochemically.
findings.project_inference: Do not convert functional catalogue names into demonstrated industrial installations. Preserve provenance and material inconsistencies pending native checks.

findings.observation: More than sixty chalkstone vessel fragments were recovered. Many occur in mixed later fills with earlier pottery. L 2039 contains a chalkstone fragment with pottery assigned exclusively to Middle Roman; Reed retains survival from the earlier phase as an alternative. Internally lathe-cut, externally hand-carved mugs occur with matching cores. No kalal jars, plates, chalk tabletops, bases or ossuaries occur in the excavated assemblage. Stoppers do not fit accompanying vessels. Catalogue and plate entries include uncertain identifications, mixed bucket dates and a mug from a homogeneous Middle Roman bucket (Plate no. 12).
findings.author_interpretation: Reed proposes a household workshop from cores and flakes, frequent use in Period I (0–135 CE), and possible later use. He explicitly says the assemblage does not settle ritual-purity motives, priestly households, Pharisaic affiliation or technological preference.
findings.project_inference: Chalkstone alone does not establish a pre-70 CE deposit or priestly identity. Retain possible survival or later use and the broad Period I range.

findings.observation: Glass composition was not tested; weathering classifications are subjective and soil-dependent. Early Roman glass includes a possible Hellenistic survivor. Few Middle Roman fragments prevent firm domestic/synagogue comparison. The lamp catalogue includes matching rim types without handles and explicitly acknowledges misidentified bowls. Simple bracelets derive their dates from contexts. Glass Plate L heading says 1–13 but includes 14; registration 80630 occurs as Late Roman J:19 and Early Arab O:17; Glass B:3 prints V.1.71, whereas Appendix B places the same item in IV.1.71.
findings.author_interpretation: Fischer retains transport and differential preservation as alternatives for thick early glass. She proposes nearby production/trade and no resident glassblower, without identifying a supplier. Increased fragments can reflect breakage rather than increased vessel use; some stylistic changes and space-use claims are interpretations.
findings.project_inference: Record vessel types and published context dates independently. Neither weathering nor fragment abundance establishes age, consumption volume, a workshop, or secure ritual lamp use. Preserve catalogue inconsistencies.

findings.observation: Metal publication samples a larger assemblage. Lamp filler and several adornments came from high or noncritical fills. The finger-ring inscription/script remains undeciphered. Five nearby shuttles support a domestic textile concentration; the two distinct loom weights came from later fills with pre-Roman material. Ceramic inkwell R80741 has no visible ink residue and catalogue locus 1009 (or 1005?) Period III. R80462 stamp seal comes from I–II fill, while the scarab/torso come from later fills containing much earlier material. Unstratified imported fills were not sifted. Narrative p.347 calls E:4 an iron adze, but catalogue p.366 identifies E:3 as adze and E:4 as bronze bell. Narrative p.347 calls E:8 the fitting; catalogue p.366 assigns E:8 pin/needle and E:9 fitting. C:1 is called Period III in narrative p.345 and Period IV in catalogue p.362.
findings.author_interpretation: Authors propose a small box/cabinet key, chandelier chain, apotropaic adornment, and pre-Roman dates for several residual items. Inkwells could reflect legal/business writing; a resident scribe and commercial use remain hypotheses. Peskowitz rejects sufficient evidence for a commercial textile workshop.
findings.project_inference: Functional labels, religious interpretations, earlier typological dates and conjectured business activity require separate records. Lack of beads is affected by excavation location and unsifted fill. Native plates can resolve item numbering but cannot independently resolve date or use.

findings.observation: The coin study revises Raynor readings using both excavation seasons. Early coins are worn, some occur with third-century coins. Antipas coin 14 dates 28/29 CE but comes from L1006; Appendix B lists mixed ER, MR and LR pottery in its bucket. Jovian coin70 has a Period IV context. Arab–Byzantine coins occur in surface fills and repaired floor makeup. Chart11 reports 34 transitional coins; narrative/conclusions repeatedly report 32. Catalogue89–123 excluding91 supplies 34, including four entries classed as imitations (89,90,107,114), whereas prose describes two imitations plus30 pre-reform coins. C23 is assigned I.2.1027 in coin catalogue but I.2.2017 bucket49 in Appendix B. Catalogue126 prints 1254–1361; narrative p.383 prints 1354–1361. Coin67/68 catalogue dates 346–350 and narrative 348–350. Catalogue totals and original 136 coins/10 unidentified/one modern tally require reconciliation.
findings.author_interpretation: Bijovsky regards a363 abandonment and circa700 ending as plausible explanations, with contemporaneous circulation and reform-date limitations discussed. Footnote12 p.382 explicitly retains copper circulation beyond reform as possible pending contextual study. Her trade orientation revises the earlier isolation argument. Lack of early coins does not fix circulation of Jannaeus issues.
findings.project_inference: Do not treat coin mint dates as construction dates, mixed-locus residuals as sealed deposits, or absence of post-reform coins as a universal hard terminus. Preserve report discrepancies and the revised nature of the conclusions.

findings.project_inference: Keep directly excavated passage/chamber/pit distinctions and bucket-level dates. Early–Middle Roman fill cannot independently date cutting or prove a pre-revolt refuge.
